title: How Democrats Won the 2026 Midterms (And Made History in Michigan)
paragraphs: November third, twenty twenty-six. Election night. At the White House, dinner was… Cheesecake Factory takeout. A staffer posted a photo of the bag, with the words: eating good on a big day.

By the next morning, dinner was the least surprising part of the night. Democrats had won the House. They had won the Senate. And Republican Senator Ted Cruz said it was not simply a blue wave… it was a blue tsunami.
And in Michigan, a doctor who had never held elected office became the first Muslim ever elected to the United States Senate. So how did all of this happen? Let's break it down.

First, the scoreboard. Democrats were on track for more than two hundred and fifty House seats. In the Senate, Democrats and their allies reached at least fifty-four, with Alaska and Mississippi still counting.
They flipped Senate seats from Maine to Ohio. They even won a Senate race in Texas, for the first time since nineteen eighty-eight.

Now, to be fair, midterms are usually rough for the president's party. Since nineteen forty-six, it has lost about twenty-five House seats in an average midterm. This year, the losses were much bigger than that.

So why did it happen? Well, that depends on who you ask. Vice President JD Vance gave the shortest answer. The reason we lost, he said, is the war. He meant the war with Iran, which many blamed for higher gas prices.
Other Republicans pointed at prices and tariffs. One Nebraska Republican put it simply: gas prices are high. Ted Cruz blamed the cost of living.

President Trump had a different theory. He wasn't on the ballot. And, he said, if I was, we would have won. The next day, the White House posted a reminder for everyone. Trump is still your president. Thank you for your attention to this matter.
Democrats, meanwhile, had leaned on one simple message. Things cost too much. And this year, a lot of voters agreed.
But the most talked-about winner of the night was in Michigan. His name is Abdul El-Sayed. He's forty-two, the son of Egyptian immigrants, and he grew up in the Detroit suburbs.

He studied at the University of Michigan, became a Rhodes Scholar at Oxford, earned a medical degree from Columbia, and taught epidemiology there. Then he came home, to lead public health in Detroit, and later in Wayne County.
In twenty eighteen, he ran for governor. And he lost the primary, by double digits.
This year, he tried again, this time for the Senate. In the August primary, outside groups spent about nine dollars against him for every dollar spent for him. He won anyway, by less than one point.

Then the general election got ugly. Trump and Vance attacked him hard. Vance called him very, very evil. Critics, including some Democrats, slammed his views on Israel and Gaza. And two days before the election, his own primary rival endorsed the Republican, Mike Rogers.
And then Michigan voted. El-Sayed beat Rogers, and became the first Muslim ever elected to the United States Senate.

His victory speech came with jokes. To President Trump, he said: you could just go on and call me Senator. And to the vice president, he said: JD, habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you're constitutionally obligated to swear me in, in January. Habibi, by the way, is Arabic for my dear.
Of course, the internet had a field day. Elon Musk, who had spent hundreds of millions of dollars backing Republicans, posted: data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.
And that Cheesecake Factory dinner? Earlier, Barack Obama had joked that the White House renovations looked like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. So the takeout bag was a cheeky reply.

So what happens now? In January, Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. But President Trump still has the veto. And he already has a plan. I'd just veto everything, he said, and they're not gonna want that.
Republicans are now arguing about what went wrong. Democrats are arguing about what their win really means. And in two years, everyone gets to do it all over again.

As for Abdul El-Sayed? In January, he'll raise his right hand, and take the oath. And the man presiding over the Senate… is JD Vance. Habibi. So, what was the biggest surprise of election night for you? Tell me in the comments.
